title: The Seizure over the Intercom
text:
In 1964 the murder of Kitty Genovese in New York was reported as a crime many neighbors had witnessed without acting. Later reporting showed that account was exaggerated, but it moved two young psychologists, John Darley and Bibb Latane, to ask a careful question: does the presence of others make each person less likely to help?

At New York University they invited students to discuss the problems of college life over an intercom, each in a separate booth, supposedly to protect privacy. Some students believed they were talking with one other person, others that the group had three or six members. In fact the other voices were recordings. Early on, one voice mentioned a tendency to have seizures. Later in the conversation that voice began to stammer, choke and ask for help, then went silent.

When students thought they were the only one who could hear, about 85 percent left their booth to get help before the seizure ended. When they thought four others were also listening, only about 31 percent did. Those who did not act were not indifferent; many were visibly anxious. But with others present, responsibility seemed to be shared out until no one felt it was theirs.
lesson: In a group, everyone assumes someone else will act. If you see someone in trouble, act as if you are the only one there, and when you need help, point at one specific person.
location: New York University, New York, USA
source: Darley, J. M., and Latane, B. (1968). Bystander intervention in emergencies: Diffusion of responsibility. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 8(4), 377-383.
